feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $f'(x) = 0$, then use $f''$ to pick the trough.

byKey.max: $x = -1$ is the other stationary point. $f''(-1) = -18 < 0$, so it is the peak.
byKey.value: $-15$ is the value $f(2)$. The question asks for $x$.

explain.text: $f'(x) = 6x^2 - 6x - 12 = 6(x - 2)(x + 1)$, so the stationary points are $x = 2$ and $x = -1$. $f''(x) = 12x - 6$ is 18 at $x = 2$: a local minimum, with $f(2) = -15$.

items.prose: A bond costs £98. At today's yield its price has slope $P'(y) = -250$.
items.question: What is its modified duration?

byKey.slope: That is the slope. Divide it by the price to get the duration.
byKey.flipped: You divided the price by the slope. Duration is the slope over the price: $\tfrac{250}{98}$.

explain.text: $D = -\tfrac{P'(y)}{P(y)} = \tfrac{250}{98} = 2.55$. So a rise of 0.01 in yield cuts the price by about 2.55%.

items.prose: An order of $q$ shares earns an expected £0.03 a share, less market impact of $0.0000015q^2$ pounds. So $\pi(q) = 0.03q - 0.0000015q^2$.
items.question: What is the largest expected profit, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $\pi'(q) = 0$, then put that $q$ back into $\pi$.

byKey.size: 10,000 is the best order size. The question asks for the profit there.
byKey.no-cost: £300 is the gross edge at 10,000 shares. Subtract the impact cost, £150.
byKey.zero: Profit is 0 at 20,000 shares, where impact eats the whole edge. The best size is half that.

items.prose: Use L’Hôpital’s rule as many times as it takes.
items.question: Find $\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{x^2}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. After one round the form is still $\tfrac{0}{0}$; apply the rule again.

byKey.stop-early: After one round you had $\tfrac{2\sin 2x}{2x}$, still $\tfrac{0}{0}$. Apply the rule again.
byKey.no-chain: That is the limit for $1 - \cos x$. The chain rule brings out a 2 each round: $2 \times 2 = 4$ on top.

explain.text: One round gives $\tfrac{2\sin 2x}{2x}$, still $\tfrac{0}{0}$. A second gives $\tfrac{4\cos 2x}{2} \to 2$. Near 0, $1 - \cos 2x$ is about $2x^2$.

items.prose: A bet pays 3 to 1 ($b = 3$) and wins with probability $p = 0.3$. The Kelly fraction is $f^* = p - \dfrac{q}{b}$.
items.question: What fraction of your bankroll should you stake? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $q = 0.7$ and divide it by $b = 3$.

byKey.p-minus-q: You left out $b$. The bet pays 3 to 1, so subtract $\tfrac{0.7}{3}$.
byKey.edge: 0.2 is the expected profit per £1, $pb - q$. Kelly divides it by $b$.
byKey.p: You staked the chance of winning. The losing chance pulls the stake down.

explain.text: $f^* = 0.3 - \tfrac{0.7}{3} = 0.0667$. Equivalently $\tfrac{pb - q}{b} = \tfrac{0.2}{3}$. A long shot with an edge still deserves only a small stake.

items.prose: A bond is priced at £100 with $P'(y) = -450$. The yield falls by 0.02, so the tangent estimate of the new price is £109.
items.question: Where is the true new price?

options.why: You reversed the bend. The price curve lies above its tangent, so the true price beats the estimate.
The tangent is exact only at today's yield. Over a move of 0.02 the curve bends away from it.

options.text: It depends on whether the yield rises or falls
options.why: The curve lies above its tangent on both sides. Either way, the true price is above the estimate.

feedback.correct: Convexity puts the true price above the tangent.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Picture the curve and its tangent at today's yield.

explain.text: A bond's price curve bends upward, so it lies above every tangent. The tangent's £109 is an underestimate, by about $\tfrac{1}{2}P''(\Delta y)^2$.

items.prose: $f(x) = x^3 - 3x$ on the closed interval $-2 \le x \le 3$.
items.question: What is the largest value of $f$ on this interval?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the stationary values with both ends.

byKey.local-max: $f(-1) = 2$ is the local maximum. The right end, $f(3) = 18$, is higher.
byKey.left-end: $f(-2) = -2$ is the smallest value, tied with $f(1)$. Check the right end.

explain.text: Stationary points: $f(-1) = 2$ and $f(1) = -2$. Ends: $f(-2) = -2$ and $f(3) = 18$. The largest value is 18, at an end.

items.prose: Interest of 10% a year is compounded $n$ times a year.
items.question: Find $\lim_{n \to \infty} \left(1 + \dfrac{0.1}{n}\right)^n$. Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take logs, use the rule on $\tfrac{\ln(1 + 0.1u)}{u}$, then undo the log.

byKey.one: You let $\tfrac{0.1}{n}$ vanish first and read $1^n$ as 1. The power grows at the same time, so the form $1^\infty$ needs care.
byKey.simple: 1.1 is compounding once a year. More frequent compounding earns interest on interest.
byKey.e: That is $e^1$. The log tends to 0.1, so the limit is $e^{0.1}$.

explain.text: The log is $\tfrac{\ln(1 + 0.1u)}{u}$ with $u = \tfrac{1}{n} \to 0$. The rule gives $\tfrac{0.1}{1 + 0.1u} \to 0.1$, so the limit is $e^{0.1} = 1.1052$.
